title: AI Risk Management: Owners, Controls, and Audit Evidence (2026)

questions.question: In Failure Shape 1 (the contract reviewer at an insurer), what was the actual audit finding?
options: The team never wrote down a consequence level for the feature
The classification was correct, but the stated human-review control never actually operated as designed
The model's accuracy was below the required threshold for legal text — and applies unchanged even when the lesson's stated preconditions fail
No risk owner had ever been named for the feature
questions.explanation: The L1 classification and 'lawyer reviews before it goes out' control were correctly designed on paper. In practice, a junior associate rubber-stamped ~80% of summaries within the same window the LLM produced them — a confirmation-bias loop, not a real review. The audit finding was that the evidence showed the control as defined did not run.

questions.question: Which consequence level requires a named human sign-off and documented rationale before an output takes effect?
options: L0 — Informational
L1 — Operational
L2 — Consequential
L3 — High-stakes
questions.explanation: L3 covers irreversible or safety-adjacent outputs with regulatory or legal exposure — medical triage, legal documents, AML alerts, production code. The table maps it to named human sign-off with documented rationale, escalated to a VP or risk owner.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what determines an AI output's consequence level?
options: Which model generated the output
The output's downstream effect on a decision, not a property of the model itself
The benchmark score the model achieved during evaluation, because one plausible output is sufficient production evidence
How much the API call for that output cost
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that consequence level is a property of the output's downstream effect, not the model. That's why events like a new downstream consumer or a change in reversibility should trigger re-classification even when the model hasn't changed at all.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say an undated policy exception is one of the most common audit findings?
options: Because exceptions are always illegal under ISO 42001
Because without an expiry, the exception silently becomes permanent instead of being periodically re-justified
Because policy exceptions require board-level sign-off in every case, before defining the measurement, acceptance threshold, or rollback path
Because undated exceptions cannot be logged in any system
questions.explanation: A written exception without an expiry date is never forced back into review. The lesson's audit-sample data found the median age of an undated exception was 11 months at the time an auditor flagged it — nobody had been forced to re-justify the risk.

questions.question: In Failure Shape 3 (the prompt workshop), why did the auditor reject the shared notion page as a risk register?
options: It contained too few use cases to be statistically meaningful
It had no schema — no field for consequence level, owner, evidence type, or exception status — so no row could be audited
It was stored in a wiki instead of a spreadsheet
None of the forty prompt templates had been tested for accuracy — and applies unchanged even when the lesson's stated preconditions fail
questions.explanation: The auditor's finding was structural: a backlog of rich prose with no schema cannot be audited at any volume, while an empty register that has the right fields is still auditable because the auditor can verify no use cases were deployed off-register.

questions.question: Which event does the lesson list as a trigger that should force a consequence-level re-classification?
options: The model provider releases a new model version with the same API, with no need to inspect intermediate results or test edge cases
The output gains a new downstream consumer, such as a CRM RAG tool being wired into a quoting workflow
The team's on-call rotation changes
The cost per token for the model decreases
questions.explanation: A new downstream consumer is one of three explicit reclassification triggers, alongside a change in the data the output influences and a change in reversibility. The CRM RAG example is exactly this: informational suggestions quietly became inputs to pricing decisions with no governance change.
